nameStory: The swamp rose gets its straightforward name from its favorite hangout spot - wet, marshy areas where other roses fear to tread. While most of its rose cousins prefer drier ground, this tough beauty has adapted to life with wet feet, earning it the "swamp" designation that immediately tells you where to look for it.
description: Swamp rose is a medium-sized wild rose shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall, thriving in wetlands across New England. Like other wild roses, it produces classic five-petaled pink flowers in early summer, followed by bright red rose hips in fall. This native shrub forms colonies through underground runners, creating natural thickets along pond edges and in marshy areas. Its thorny stems and compound leaves give it the unmistakable rose family look, but its love of wet soils sets it apart from most other roses.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five delicate pink petals surround a bright yellow center, measuring about 2 inches across. The flowers have a light, sweet fragrance and bloom in clusters of 1-3 flowers from June to July.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 oval leaflets arranged feather-like along the stem. Each leaflet has fine teeth along the edges and feels smooth on top with a slightly fuzzy underside.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies in consistently wet areas like pond edges, swamps, and stream banks. Stems are noticeably less thorny than most wild roses, with scattered curved prickles rather than dense armament.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red, round rose hips about the size of a small cherry persist into winter. They feel firm when fresh and have a tart, slightly sweet taste that birds love.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are green to reddish-brown with scattered curved thorns that are less intimidating than those of multiflora rose. Older stems develop grayish bark that peels in thin strips.

habitat: Look for swamp rose along pond shores, stream banks, marshes, and wet meadows throughout New England. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soils that would be too soggy for most other roses, often growing alongside cattails, red-winged blackbird nesting areas, and other wetland plants. You'll frequently find it forming natural hedgerows at the transition zone between open water and drier upland areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late April to May, with the distinctive compound rose leaves helping identify it before flowers appear.
seasonality.summer: Pink flowers bloom from June through July, creating fragrant displays that attract bees and butterflies to wetland edges.
seasonality.fall: Bright red rose hips ripen in September and October, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping, leaving the thorny stems visible.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red rose hips on bare thorny stems make identification possible, along with the characteristic wetland habitat and colonial growth pattern.

funFact: Swamp rose is the host plant for the blinded sphinx moth, whose caterpillars are perfectly camouflaged to look like rose stems complete with fake thorns - they even sway like twigs when threatened!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Carolina rose, but swamp rose's wetland habitat is the best clue - if your feet are getting wet, it's likely swamp rose rather than Carolina rose which prefers drier ground. Remember: "Swamp rose loves swampy toes!"
compareHints: Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies. Swamp rose also has fewer and less intimidating thorns than most of its rose relatives, making it one of the more approachable wild roses to examine up close.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
